That Iblis is a fallen angel is abundantly clear from verse 34, "I said to the angels, 'Fall prostrate before Adam.'" Thus, the command to fall prostrate was directed to the angels. Had Iblis been other than an angel, therefore, he would not have been expected to obey such command. The fact that Iblis was held responsible for disobedience is clear evidence that he is a fallen angel. Some students of the Qur'an maintain that Iblis is a jinn; that angels do not disobey divine commands. They base their argument on verses 12 of sura Al-A'raf (No.7) and 76 of sura Sad (No. 38) which state,

Iblis said, "I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from mud."

verse 15 of sura Al-Rahman (No. 55):

He created jinn from blazing fire

and verse 50 of sura Al-Kahf (No. 18):

I said to the angels, "Fall prostrate before Adam." They fell prostrate, except Iblis; he was a jinn; he disobeyed the command of his Lord.

However, the statement that Iblis was created from fire does not necessarily mean that he was different from the angels (who supposedly were created from light). The common belief that the angels were created from light is not supported by a single verse in the Qur'an; nowhere in the Qur'an are we told that the angels were created from light. If the source of this general belief is a Hadith or a tradition of which this commentator is unaware, this still does not necessitate that Iblis was not an angel. The Qur'an commonly refers to the various stages of man's creation [dust (3:59; 18:37; 22:5; 30:20; 38:71; 38:76; 17:61), clay (6:2; 7:12; 23:12; 32:7; 37:11; 38:76; 53:46), mud (35:11; 40:67), drop of semen (16:4; 23:13-14; 15:26; 15:28; 15:33; 55:14), hanging clot (75:37; 76:2; 80:19; 96:2)]. Original Sin!?

Islam holds that each individual is solely responsible for his or her deeds (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38). This doctrine applies of course to Adam, as stated in verse 37 of sura Al-Baqarah. Adam and Eve sinned (verse 36), and they alone were held responsible. The concept of "repentance" was taught to Adam (verse 37); he exercised this concept, and his repentance was accepted by the Almighty. Thus, Adam was completely exonerated; his sin was forgiven and erased. "Original sin" (a foreign concept introduced into "Christianity"), therefore, is an unacceptable doctrine in Islam; unacceptable to the all-encompassing justice of God. Likewise, the commonly believed concept in the Judaeo-Christian world that Adam and Eve's sin of "eating the apple" refers euphemistically to sexual intercourse is unacceptable to Islam. This idea has caused millions to believe that sexual relations, even between a man and wife, are inherently sinful, and it is in part responsible for much of the sexual aberration and perversion which plagues the West.

IN THE NAME OF GOD, THE COMPASSIONATE, THE MERCIFUL

My mercy encompasses all things. But I will designate it for those who maintain righteousness, observe charity, and believe in My revelations; Those who follow the messenger, the illiterate prophet (Muhammad) whom they find written in their Torah as well as the Gospel. He enjoins upon them but righteousness, and prohibits but evil; he permits for them but the good, and forbids for them but the bad; he unburdens them and breaks the chains which bind them. Indeed, those who believe in him, honor him, support him, and follow the light which was revealed through him, shall be the winners. Say (O Muhammad), "O mankind, I am the messenger of God to you; all of you."
(Sura Al-A'raf 7:156-158)

by Dr. 'Abdul-Halim Mahmud
Grand Shaykh of Al-Azhar

The Origin of
Islamic Jurisprudence

What some have erroneously termed "Islamic sects" are merely branches of one tree. There is but one school of jurisprudence in Islam, that based on the life and personal conduct of the prophet Muhammad (God's blessings and peace be upon him). It is from the extensive record of his exemplary life that the four well-known branches of Islamic jurisprudence evolved. The very initiation of these branches was approved by the Prophet himself. Thus, when he appointed Mu'adh b. Jabal as a viceroy in Yemen, the Prophet asked him, "How will you rule?" Mu'adh replied, "According to the Qur'an." The Prophet said, "What if you do not find a related rule in the Qur'an?" Mu'adh replied, "I will rule according to the sunnah (the Prophet's tradions)." The Prophet proceeded, "What if you do not find the ruling there?" Mu'adh said, "Then, I will have to depend on my personal thought and reasoning (ajtahidu)." The Prophet is reported to have been pleased and approved of Mu'adh's line of thinking.
In this article, the grand imam of Azhar reports on the origin and nature of the one tree of Islamic jurisprudence.

The final messenger of God (may God bestow peace and blessings upon him) practiced Islam as the Almighty wanted it to be practiced. He applied Islam to all aspects of his life; his actions, reactions, talk, feelings, and his daily conduct were all governed by Islam. The Prophet's companions followed his example very closely. This example of the Prophet was transmitted to us from his companions to their contemporaries and then onwards from generation to generation.

The companions of the Prophet explained the Islamic way of life as they saw the Prophet live it. They narrated everything he did or said with regard to all kinds of circumstances. As the Muslim nation expanded, the Muslims transmitted these traditions to the new areas. Eventually, many outstanding scholars evolved who specialized in researching, collecting, and recording the Prophet's traditions. Most of those scholars observed the highest

principles of scientific investigations to assure the accuracy and truthfulness of their sources. Their methods of collection and authentication of the Prophet's life have been highly esteemed by even the modern historians.

The Prophet's example was consistent with regard to certain specific situations. In other situations, however, he deliberately varied his mode of behavior. The situations where he was consistent include all the fard (the obligatory rites of worship). These encompass such rites as the method of fasting, the recitation of Qur'an during the salat, and the kneeling for "tashuhhud" recitation.

The variability in the Prophet's example was observed only with regard to the nonobligatory functions which are designated today as "sunnah." Thus, his conduct did not follow one specific methodology in such sunnahs as reciting supplications between the initial takbir of salat (saying, "Allah Akbar") and the opening sura (Al-Fatihah), and in his supplications as he fell prostrate in salat, and in the manner of placing the arms and hands during salat, and so forth. Such variations were observed also in many situations of daily life involving commerce, crimes, loans, usury, and personal relations. it is only around these variations in sunnah that the four branches of jurisprudence evolved. No differences whatsoever exist among the opinions of the imams Al-Shafi'i, Malik, Abu Hanifah, and ibn Hanbal concerning the obligatory duties. Their differences are found only in their personal interpretation and reasoning with regard to the nonobligatory actions and behavior of the Prophet.

These non-doctrinal differences of opinion among the four great imams have been grossly exaggerated by various groups who sought to create imaginary sects or divisions within Islam. Such exaggerations were intended mainly to divert the Muslims from their basic Islamic doctrines and, hence, from establishing the perfect society as inculcated by Islam. It was such groups who created, for example, the question of whether one should fold or unfold the arms while standing in salat. In the folding situation, the worshiper places the left hand on the stomach and the right hand on the back of the left hand. In the unfolding situation, the worshiper simply lets the arms hang down freely on the sides. This minor issue was magnified by some researchers beyond reasonable proportions, and led to lengthy and hot debates in certain Muslim countries. These arguments were finally terminated when one enlightened scholar raised the following questions to those involved in the controversy:
1. If the worshiper stood in salat with his arms extended straight forward, would that nullify the prayer?
2. If the arms were lifted completely upward, would that nullify the prayer?

THE ORIGIN OF ISLAMIC JURISPRUDENCE

3. If the arms were folded, would the prayer be nullified?
4. If the arms hang down on the sides, would that nullify the prayer?
When the debators unanimously agreed that the answer to each of these questions was "No", they realized the insignificance of their differences.

This question of placing one's arms during the salat prayer is a typical example of the subjects in which the great imams of jurisprudence expressed varied opinions. It is such differences of opinion, originating from the traditions of the Prophet, that became the basis of the branches in Islamic jurisprudence.

Clearly, all these branches, reflecting different personal interpretations, belong to one and the same tree. All the imams of jurisprudence had but a single model from which they derived their opinions. Only ignorance and narrow-mindedness would create separate schools of jurisprudence out of the one school, namely, the school of prophet Muhammad (God's peace and blessings be upon him). It is heartening to note that the era of false divisions within the school of Islamic jurisprudence has passed. It is a rarity nowadays to meet a Muslim who describes himself as a Shafi'i, Maliki, Hanafi, or Hanbali; the trend has been towards the one essential description: Muslim.

Who Qualifies as a Mujtahid?

By a mujtahid here is meant one who is scholarly qualified to set new rules and regulations to be followed by the Muslims everywhere. Some scholars have contended that the door of ijtihad (personal thought and reasoning which leads to new rules) has been closed; that the last mujtahids were the four well-known imams. Other scholars maintain that the door of ijtihad is always open. Some among the latter group, however, talk about ijtihad as if it were attainable by anyone. It is inconceivable that God's grace was limited to the four great imams with regard to ijtihad, since new circumstances are founded with each generation of humans. Therefore, any Muslim who satisfies certain exacting requirements can contribute to the rules and regulations known as Islamic jurisprudence, i.e., become a mujtahid. These requirements include:
1. Mastery of the Arabic language: The great imams of jurisprudence (e.g. Malik and Al-Shafi'i) were unrivaled masters of the Arabic linguistic sciences.
2. Memorization of the Qur'an, with full awareness of the complete message and regulations therein. This includes a high degree of knowledge of the various Qur'anic sciences such as the circumstances associated with the revelation of each verse or group of verses. Although the Qur'an was revealed for the guidance of all the people in all places and at all times, knowledge of the specific circumstances of revelation does help in reaching

'Abdul-Halim Mahmud

the correct interpretation.
3. Knowledge of the spoken sunnah, as well as the practical traditions of the Prophet (God's peace and blessings be upon him).
These requirements form the basic background needed by a Muslim before he or she can contribute correctly to Islamic jurisprudence.

The seriousness and the awesomeness of responsiblity in issuing new rules of jurisprudence can be appreciated if we reflect upon some of the Prophet's teachings in this regard. In Sahih Al-Shaykhan (well-known record of Hadith), the Prophet (may God bestow peace and blessings upon him) is reported as saying, "Whoever fabricates false rules from my teachings shall be committing a gross offense." Abu Hurayrah reported the Prophet's saying, "Whoever establishes a righteous tradition shall receive a reward equal to that due to all followers of such tradition, without reduction in their rewards. And whoever establishes an evil tradition shall incur sins equal to all the sins of those who follow such evil tradition, without reducing their guilt (reported in Sahih Muslim).

The overall purpose of ijtihad can be divided into 2 areas:
1. Establishing rules of Islamic jurisprudence relating to matters which took place during the Prophet's time. In this case, the purpose would be to find the Prophet's judgment regarding the matter in question. An example here would be the search for the exact manner of making ablution (wudu'), as performed by the Prophet (may God bestow peace and blessings upon him).
2. Establishing rules of Islamic jurisprudence dealing with current matters which did not exist during the Prophet's time. Even here, the rule-making process must depend on the Prophet's example through Qiyas (analogy).
The Qur'an and the sunnah of the holy Prophet provide an unlimited array of situations which can be used directly or indirectly in establishing current rules of Islamic jurisprudence. Thus, the Muslim never lacks the reference materials he needs to establish a given rule. Under all circumstances, the mujtahid must be a "follower," rather than an "initiator." For the Prophet's instructions to the mujtahids are, "you shall follow, not invent" when dealing with rules of Islamic jurisprudence.

Finally, it must be pointed out that ijtihad cannot succeed through knowledge alone. A mujtahid must be characterized first and foremost by a high standard of piety and righteousness. All the great imams who contributed positively to Islamic jurisprudence had in common a high level of genuine piety. Thus, the rules they have established for us represent no less than guidance from God to His sincere servants. Knowledge alone can never invoke such divine guidance, for God tells us, "only those who stand by God shall receive right guidance." (Qur'an 3:101).
notes: This is the end of 'The Origin of Islamic Jurisprudence' article (pages 138-141).

Islamic Concentrates

The Aphorisms
of Salamah Al-Radi : 2

These aphorisms, with their esoteric connotations, are derived from the Qur'an, the sunna, teachings of the great imams, and the principles of Sufism. Published for the first time in English, these particular aphorisms are valuable pieces of advice delivered by one of the greatest Sufis of all time, Shaykh Salamah Al-Radi, to his dervishes.

11. My beloved in (the cause of) God: If anyone of you wishes God to heed his prayers, he shall first heed God's commands. When you heed Him, He heeds you.

12. My beloved ones: Whoever claims to have acquired dignity on his own, reveals but sinful pride. But whoever humbles himself before his Master, derives his dignity from his Lord. When The Reality sees you humbling yourself before Him, He permits no humiliation to ever touch you; He guarantees your dignity.

13. My beloved in (the cause of) God: Once your hearts are fully content with your Master, you enter the court of His grace. For as long as you are hesitant, you remain strangers to Him. He is only with those who are fully with him.

14. O you beloved ones: If your heart truly loves your Master, it will not grieve over parting with anything else. So long as you grieve over parting with other than your Master, this should be your indicator that you are not yet in His court. Rather, you would be in the court of whatever diverted you from your Master.

15. O you beloved ones: If you are saddened by the people's criticism, and rejoice when they flatter you, beware. This would indicate that your ego is still alive and thus still competing with the Master in His divine attributes.

THE APHORISMS OF SALAMAH AL-RADI : 2

16. O you beloved ones: If you spend your lives worshiping your Master, while at the same time being dissatisfied with Him, not humbling yourselves before His dignity, staying away from His company, keeping your thoughts with the devils and the far-removed individuals, how do you expect your worship to attain any light? It would be spiritless worship; dead.

17. O you beloved ones: You care too much for feeding vanishing shells, and pay little attention to feeding your eternal entity. Consequently, you end up with great bodies, but diminished souls.

18. O you beloved ones: Your hearts are like empty containers. You strive and even pay monies to fill them with darkness, while the light is within your reach, free of charge. Instead of helping yourselves to the light, you keep pushing your hearts further and further therefrom. Would a wise person fill his eyes with darkness, until he sees but darkness? Or, would he rather fill them with light in order to become a seer?

19. O beloved ones: The love of this life has a certain sweetness which causes intoxication of the heart. Thus, it becomes distracted from the love of its Master, and adores but illusions. This world is no more than an illusion. Therefore, you shall not imbibe this particular wine; it is far more evil than the grape's wine which masks the mind from physical objects.

20. My beloved in (the path to) God: Whenever you see one who obeys the devil & does his deeds, you shall stay clear of him; he is a devil himself. Whoever befriends him shall in turn become a devil like him.

21. O you beloved ones: Whoever is filled with goodness, nothing but goodness comes out of him. Whoever is filled with evil, nothing but evil comes out of him. How could evil ever spill out of one who is filled with goodness?

22. O you beloved ones: Whoever adorns himself with virtue exhibits but virtue. Therefore, you shall strive to become virtuous people, so that only virtuous traits may be reflected from you.

23. My beloved ones: The poor, by definition, is one who is in need. Thus, if one possesses tremendous wealth but still seeks more wealth, he is poor. He continues to labor in order to acquire more riches. If he is never satisfied, his poverty will last all his life.

THE APHORISMS OF SALAMAH AL-RADI : 2

24. O you beloved ones: Whoever seeks power tires himself, for power is beloved by all, and the people fight among themselves over it. Therefore, you should not seek power. It will seek you so long as you shun seeking it, and when anyone opposes you in this case, many will stand by you and support you.

25. My beloved ones: If anyone claims superiority over you, do not fight him. If you fight him over it, it will abandon both you and him. But if you allow him to claim superiority, it will abandon him and come to you.

26. My beloved ones: If anyone fights you over what belongs to God, you shall not fight him. God cares for whatever belongs to Him, & if you take the matter in your hands and fight over His belongings, you yourselves belong to God no more.

27. My beloved ones: You gain God's love if you are persecuted in His cause. Thus, you shall seek victory for His cause. You shall never seek victory for yourselves. If you do, you fall from your Master's grace.

28. My beloved ones: You shall persevere in the face of persecution, injustice, and tribulation. Do not ever execrate or curse. Instead, you shall be exemplars of mercy and pardon on earth, in order to earn the love of your Master. The Almighty is always with those whose hearts are broken in His cause.

29. My beloved ones: While the people are busy with the affairs of this life, you shall busy yourselves with your Master. While they are busy with the given, you shall be busy with the Giver.

30. My beloved ones: Habituate yourselves with doing good, & respond not to evil by evil. God loves the good-doers.

Islamic Concentrates

The Invocations of
'Abdullah Ansari : 2

'Abdullah Ansari, a famous Persian Sufi, was born in Herat 396 AH (1005 C.E.). It is said that one of his ancestors was a companion of the prophet Muhammad (God's blessings and peace be upon him) who moved to Herat with 'Asaf, son of Qays. Ansari's father, Abu Mansur Muhammad Ansari, became a permanent resident of Herat.

These invocations, translated into English by Sir Jogendra Singh, contain true advice to guide the Pilgrim along the path of discipleship to the temple of peace. They come from a man who himself had trodden the path and found what his heart desired.

When 'Abdullah Ansari departed from this world, he was 85 years old, leaving behind a wealth of Sufi knowledge. Among his well-known works are Risala Munajat (The Book of Prayer), Tabaqat-ul-Sufiyyah (The Book of Sufis), Zad-ul-'Arifin (Provisions of the Sufi Teachers), and Kitab-i-Israr (The Book of Mysteries).

O Lord, give me a heart
That I may pour it out in thanksgiving.
Give me life
That I may spend it
in working for the salvation of the world.

O Lord, give me that right discrimination
That the Lure of the world may cheat me no more.
Give me strength
That my faith suffer no eclipse.

O Lord, give me understanding,
That I stray not from the path.
Give me light
To avoid pitfalls.

O Lord, keep watch over me
That I stray not.
Keep me on the path of righteousness
That I escape from the pangs of repentance.

THE INVOCATIONS OF 'ABDULLAH ANSARI : 2

O Lord, judge me not by my actions.
Of Thy mercy, save me,
And make my humble efforts fruitful.

O Lord, give me a heart
Free from the flames of desire.
Give me a mind
Free from the waves of dissimulation.

O Lord, give me eyes
Which see nothing but Thy glory.
Give me a mind
That finds delight in Thy service.
Give me a soul
Drunk in the wine of Thy wisdom.

O Lord, to find Thee is my desire
But to comprehend Thee
Is beyond my strength.
Remembering Thee is solace
to my sorrowing heart,
Thoughts of Thee are my Constant Companions
I call upon Thee night and day.
The flame of Thy love glows
In the darkness of my night.

O Lord, he whom Thou killest doth not smell of blood,
And he whom Thou burnest doth not smell of smoke,

For he whom Thou burnest is happy in
The burning,
And he whom Thou killest, rejoiceth
In being killed.

O Lord, though the blue flower be poisonous
It is of Thy garden,
And if 'Abdullah be a sinner
He is of Thy people.

O Lord, when I think of Thy compassion
I feel like a crowned king;
When I think of my sins
I am as dust, nay, less than dust.

THE INVOCATIONS OF 'ABDULLAH ANSARI : 2

Life in my body pulsates only for Thee,
My heart beats in resignation to Thy will.
If on my dust a tuft of grass were
To grow
Every blade would tremble with my devotion
For Thee.

O Lord, every one desires to behold Thee,
I desire
That Thou mayest cast a glance at me.

Let me not disgrace myself.
If Thy forgiveness awaits me in the end
Lower not the standard of forgiveness
Which Thou hast unfurled.

O Lord, if Thou sendest me to Hell
I raise no protest.
And if Thou takest me to Paradise,
I go there, but not of my own choice.

If in Hell I obtain union with Thee
What care I for those who dwell in Paradise?
And were I called to Heaven without Thee
The pleasures of Paradise would then
Be worse than the fires of Hell.

O Lord, prayer at Thy gate
Is a mere formality:
Thou knowest what Thy slave desires.

O Lord, better for me to be dust,
And my name effaced
From the records of the world,
Than that Thou forget me.

He knoweth all our good and evil
Nothing is hidden from Him.
He knoweth what is best medicine
To cure the pain,
And to rescue the fallen.
Be humble, for He exalteth the humble.

I am intoxicated with love of Thee
And need no fermented wine.

THE INVOCATIONS OF 'ABDULLAH ANSARI : 2

I am Thy bird
Free from need of seed
And safe from the snare of the fowler.
In the Ka'ba and in the Temple
Thou art the object of my search.
Else I am freed
From both these places of worship.

O Lord, when the fire of separation was burning me
Why didst Thou light the fire of Hell?

Lord, when Thou wert hidden from me
The fever of life possessed me.
When Thou revealest Thyself
This fever of life departeth.

O Lord, other men are afraid of Thee
But I — I am afraid of myself,
From Thee flows good alone,
From me flows evil.

Each day I recall the day,
That is left behind.
Sorrowing over my misdeeds
The dread of my doings drives me to despair.
The thought of Thy mercy
Is the only solace of my heart.

Others fear what the morrow
May bring.
I am afraid of what happened yesterday.

O Lord, if Thou holdest me responsible for
My sins
I shall cling to Thee for Thy Grace.

I with my sin, am an insignificant atom.
Thy Grace is resplendent as the Sun.

O Lord, out of regard for Thy name,
The qualities which are Thine,
Out of regard for Thy greatness,
Listen to my cry
For Thou alone canst redeem me.

THE INVOCATIONS OF 'ABDULLAH ANSARI : 2

O Lord, intoxicate me with the wine
Of Thy love.
Place the chains of Thy slavery on
My feet;
Make me empty of all but Thy love,
And in it destroy me and bring me
Back to life.
The hunger Thou has awakened, culminates
In fulfillment.

Make my body impervious to the fires
Of Hell;
Vouchsafe to me a vision of Thee in heaven.
The spark Thou has kindled make it
Everlasting.

I think of no other,
And in Thy love care for none else.
None has a place in my heart but Thee.
My heart has become Thy abode,
It has no place for another.

O Lord, Thou cherishest the helpless
And I am helpless,
Apply Thy balm to my bleeding heart
For Thou art the physician.

O Lord, I, a beggar, ask of Thee
More than what a thousand kings may ask of Thee;
Each one has something he needs to ask of Thee,
I have come to ask Thee to give me Thyself.

If words can establish a claim I claim a crown.
But if deeds are wanted, I am as helpless as
The ant.

Urged by desire I wandered in the streets
Of good and evil,
I gained nothing except feeding the fire of desire.

As long as in me remains the breath of life
Help me, for Thou alone canst hear my prayer.

My friend, wisdom lies
In abandoning heedlessness,

THE INVOCATIONS OF 'ABDULLAH ANSARI : 2

In turning the heart away from the worldly objects,
And in gathering provision for the hereafter
Before departure from this earth.

Someone asked the Holy Prophet —
"What dost thou say concerning the things of the world?"
The Prophet said — "What can I say about them:
Things which are acquired with hard labour,
Preserved with perpetual watchfulness,
And left with regret."

My friend, the world is not a place
For enjoyment,
But a place where humanity is on trial.
The world is a mere crossing
And not an abiding city of delight.

O mendicant, man is doomed to death
And has to leave the world.

Dost thou take the world for a friend
Or foe?
If thou holdest it a friend,
Know that it will not last,
If thou holdest it to be a foe, consume it,
So that it may not last.

Behold what thou art, and whence thou
Hast come.
Beware what thou doest and whither
Thou wouldest go,
If thou treadest the path of lust and longing
Thou shalt go without fruit and without good name.

My friend, put not thy reliance
On three things:
On heart, on time and on life.
The heart is easily tempted,
Time is always in a state of flux,
The sands of life run out.
